study.title: Jeremiah 43 The refusal of the word and judgment that reaches Egypt
study.overview: After hearing the warning of Jeremiah to remain in Judah, the people led by Johanan reject the word of the LORD, accuses the prophet of lying and takes Jeremiah and Baruch himself to Egypt. In response, God speaks again in Tafnes and announces that Nebuchadnezzar, whom he calls his servant, will invade Egypt, destroy his sanctuaries and reduce his political and religious forces. The chapter shows that fleeing to Egypt does not bring security when trust in the Lord has already been abandoned.

outline.title: The rejection of the word and the escape to Egypt
outline.explanation: Jeremiah ends speaking, but the leaders and the people reject their message, accuse him of falsehood and disobey the divine command to stay in the land of Judah. Even bringing Jeremiah, Baruch, men, women and children, they cross into Egypt and arrive at Tafnes, revealing that the decision was already taken against the will of God.

outline.title: Sign in Tafnes and Babylonian invasion announcement
outline.explanation: In Tafnes, the Lord sends Jeremiah to hide great stones as a sign before the Jews. The stones announce that Nebuchadnezzar will establish his throne and his tent there, that is, his authority shall attain Egypt. The judgment will be comprehensive: death, captivity, sword, and fire upon the houses of the Egyptian gods.

outline.title: Fall of images and temples of Egypt
outline.explanation: The announcement concludes with the destruction of the statues of Beth-shemesh and the fire of the houses of the gods of Egypt. Egyptian idolatry does not resist the God of Israel, which shows his dominion also outside the land of Judah.

study.context: The notes indicate that Tafnes was on Egypt's entrance route, in a strategic position on the northeast border. The chapter also mentions Beth-Semes, understood in the notes as "home of the sun," an Egyptian cult center associated with the sun as the main deity. The text describes a time when Jewish leaders, by disobedience, take the prophet to Egypt, but the Lord continues to speak there, showing that his word is not restricted to a territory.
study.theology: The chapter teaches the gravity of unbelief that disguises itself as prudence. The leaders call the lie what God had said, and their rebellion is born of pride, not of lack of information. Also appears the sovereignty of God over the nations: he calls Nebuchadnezzar his servant and uses it as an instrument of judgment. The Lord not only disciplines his people, but also overthrows the false security of Egyptian idols. The destruction of temples and images shows that the religious and political power of nations is subject to divine rule. For a Protestant evangelical reading, this text also recalls that disobeying the word of God never produces true refuge; the only security is in listening and trusting in the Lord.

scholarViews.insight: Joanna and the other leaders betrayed the commitment made earlier by refusing to trust the Lord's reply through Jeremiah.
Opposition to the prophet is born of pride, for they deny that the message comes from God and insist on following their own desire to go to Egypt.
The order to destroy the images of Beth-shemesh shows the fall of the main center of the sun worship in Egypt, a sign of judgment against idolatry.

questions: In which areas have I treated the word of God as inconvenient, trying to disqualify it instead of obeying it?
Which I seek as a safety solution, even when God has guided me in another direction?
How does this chapter confront my confidence in human resources, religious structures or symbols of power?
study.practice: Read the chapter as an examination of obedience. Identify a concrete decision in which you already know what God requires, but still tries to justify another way out. Confess this resistance to God, ask for a humble heart and take a specific step of obedience this week. Also, pray for leaders and the church so that they do not replace God's voice for convenience, fear or pride.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not clarify why Baruch was accused in 43:3; therefore, any reason beyond the statement that it is not known should remain undefined. It was also not possible to detail more about Beth-Semes beyond what the notes provide, and the historical context was limited to what appears in the data excerpts.
